title: The hymn that bows to everything
hookLine: namah, namah, namah: a hymn that faces an angry god with a strung bow, and starts by bowing
carry: the rudram bows to shiva in everything
tomorrow: a woman judges a debate between two great teachers. whose garland wilts first?

lines: A GOD WITH A STRUNG BOW.
cards: Said once, it's a bow, a word of homage. Said over and over in a steady chant, it becomes a rhythm you can feel in the floor. The hymn built on it faces a god who is not, at first, gentle.
Rudra stands with his bow strung and an arrow ready. And the hymn doesn't run, and doesn't argue. It bows: to the arrow, to the bow, to the anger itself.
Today's summit sit climbs back to the Rudram, and the night the year spent awake with Shiva.

teach.h: BOW TO THE ANGER. ASK THE ARROW TO SOFTEN.
teach.b: The Rudram comes from the Yajur Veda. In paraphrase, it opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrow, and to his arms. Then it asks: make that arrow gentle; let your kind form be turned toward us.
That's the first move. Fear isn't hidden or argued away. It's bowed to, and asked to soften.
Then the hymn widens. It bows to Rudra in the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest.

teach.h: NAMAH TO THE TREES, THE RAIN, THE POTTER.
teach.b: In the trees with green hair. In the rain and in the drought, in the well and in the foam on the water.

teach.h: AND TO ME: AN HONEST ASK.
teach.b: In thieves, even, and in the carpenters and the potters. Line after line, namah, until almost nothing in the world is left out of the bowing. Rudra isn't only on the mountain.
He's in the crowd, the weather and the workshop. Then its companion, often chanted right after, turns the direction. Line after line, it asks: and to me, strength, food, breath, peace, long life.
Bowing to everything, then asking honestly for what a person needs. The year carried that hymn into the dark, too.
On Maha Shivaratri, it's chanted while water pours over the linga, through a night kept awake, often without food, until the gray light comes.

teach.h: NOTHING LEFT OUT OF THE BOWING.
teach.b: That's the teaching under the hymn: Shiva isn't only on the mountain or in the temple. He is in every being, the frightening ones included.

In many homes it's still chanted on Mondays, Shiva's day, as water runs over a small linga. And it trains the eye for an ordinary day: the boss who scares you, the neighbor you'd rather avoid. Namah comes first.

how: The Sri Rudram is chanted in Shiva temples and homes, often during abhisheka, when water, milk or other offerings are poured over the linga, and through the night of Maha Shivaratri.

o: a chant sung only to drive away an angry god

s: the Rudram begins by asking Rudra to destroy enemies
it begins by bowing to his anger and asking that his arrow be made gentle.
the Rudram bows to Rudra in thieves and potters as well as in trees and rain
the bowing reaches almost everything, the workshop and the weather included.
the companion hymn only praises; it never asks for anything
it asks, line after line, and to me: strength, food, breath, peace, long life.

games.q: you're facing Rudra. his bow is strung and the arrow is ready. what does the hymn do first?
o: call on another god for protection.
bow to his anger and ask the arrow to be gentle.
list the reasons he shouldn't be angry.
games.why: the Rudram bows to the anger, the arrow and the bow, then asks that the kind form of Rudra be turned toward us. fear is bowed to, not argued away.

practice: Let the bow move outward, one thing per breath: your own body, the room, the people nearby, the weather outside, someone who makes you angry.
If something feels too hard to bow to, bow to the hard feeling instead; if you pray, say namah softly with each one.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Rudram and Shivaratri, a hymn that bows to an angry god and then to everything. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: namaḥ, a bow, homage, the word the Rudram repeats until it becomes the rhythm.

carryVoice: Your line: the Rudram bows to Shiva in everything, the arrow and the potter alike. Until tomorrow.
